procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated October 3, 1963 of the Patna High Court in Criminal Misc. Case No. 366 of 1956, ordering the Registrar of the High Court to file a complaint before the appropriate authority for the prosecution of Baban Singh and Dharichhan Kuer under s. 199 of the Indian Penal Code for making false affidavits.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Jagdish Singh and Parmhans were appellants in F. A. 301 of 1952 in the High Court at Patna. Mst. Dharichhan Kuer was respondent No. 13 in that appeal. During the pendency of the appeal a compromise was said to have been arrived at between Dharichhan Kuer on the one hand and Jagdish Singh and Parmhans on the other. Dharichhan Kuer and Jagdish Singh swore an affidavit on June 22, 1953 in support of the petition for compromise which was filed in the High Court. Baban Singh's brother identified Dharichhan Kuer before the Oath Commissioner and Rs. 4,000 were paid to Dharichhan Kuer under the terms of the compromise in the Commissioner's presence. Dharichhan Kuer also passed a receipt and her thumb impression was identified by Baban Singh's brother. The petition of compromise was filed in court on July 13, 1953. The same day Baban Singh swore an affidavit (Ex. B) denying the compromise or that his wife had received Rs. 4,000. This affidavit was filed in the High Court on July 31, 1953. On September 9, 1953 Dharichhan Kuer also filed an affidavit (Ex. A) in support of her husband. The High Court ordered the Registrar to hold an enquiry. The application under s. 476 out of which this appeal has arisen was filed during the pendency of the first appeal and was taken up for hearing after the appeal was disposed of.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Baban Singh and his wife Dharichhan Kuer appealed under s. 476-B of the Code of Criminal Procedure against the High Court's order. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order for the prosecution of the appellants.

decision.appeal_result: The appeal succeeds and is allowed.
directions: The order for the prosecution of the appellants is set aside.
The complaint, if filed, shall be withdrawn.

issue.issue_text: Whether the offence committed by the appellants by making false declarations in their affidavits fell under ss. 191/192 of the Indian Penal Code (giving/fabricating false evidence) or under s. 199 of the Indian Penal Code (false statement in a declaration).

facts: The appellants made false declarations in affidavits which were then submitted to the High Court.
The purpose of these affidavits was to influence the court's opinion regarding a compromise in a pending appeal.
law: Section 191 of the Indian Penal Code defines the offence of giving false evidence, which involves making a false statement when legally bound by an oath to state the truth. An affidavit is a declaration made under oath.

Section 192 of the Indian Penal Code defines the offence of fabricating false evidence, which includes making a document with a false statement with the intent that it may appear as evidence in a judicial proceeding and cause the court to form an erroneous opinion.
Section 199 of the Indian Penal Code deals with making a false statement in a declaration that is receivable as evidence, but it does not require the declaration to be made under oath.
application: The Court determined that an affidavit is a declaration made under oath, which brings it directly under the purview of Section 191.

Furthermore, by creating and submitting the affidavits to the High Court, the appellants intended for the false statements to appear as evidence in a judicial proceeding and mislead the court about the compromise. This action fits the definition of fabricating false evidence under Section 192.

The Court distinguished this from Section 199, which applies more broadly to declarations not necessarily made under oath. Since the false statements were in affidavits (declarations under oath) intended for use in court, the more specific offences under ss. 191/192 were applicable.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the appellants' offence of making false declarations in their affidavits fell under sections 191 and 192 of the Indian Penal Code (giving or fabricating false evidence) rather than section 199, because the affidavits were declarations made under oath and were intended to be used as evidence to mislead the court in a judicial proceeding.

issue.issue_text: Whether proceedings for giving false evidence could be initiated under s. 476 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, or whether such action was barred because the specific procedure under s. 479-A of the Code was not followed.

facts: The appellants filed affidavits in the High Court denying the receipt of money, which were later found to be false.
The High Court, believing that the special procedure under s. 479-A of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) applied to giving false evidence on oath, chose not to prosecute for that offense.

Instead, the High Court initiated proceedings under the general procedure of s. 476 CrPC, framing the offense as making a false declaration in an affidavit under s. 199 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
law: Section 479-A of the CrPC provides a special procedure for prosecuting a witness who intentionally gives or fabricates false evidence in a judicial proceeding (offenses under ss. 191/192 of the IPC).
Section 479-A(6) explicitly states that if proceedings *can* be taken under s. 479-A, then no proceedings shall be taken under the general provisions of ss. 476 to 479.

This means that for the specific offenses of a witness giving or fabricating false evidence, the special procedure of s. 479-A is mandatory and exclusive, barring the use of the general procedure under s. 476.
application: The Supreme Court first determined the nature of the appellants' offense. It held that by filing false affidavits intended to be used as evidence in court, the appellants committed the offense of giving/fabricating false evidence under ss. 191/192 of the IPC, rather than the offense of making a false declaration under s. 199.
Since the appellants were witnesses and their offense fell under ss. 191/192, the Court found that the special procedure under s. 479-A was the correct and only applicable procedure.
The High Court had failed to follow this mandatory special procedure.
Consequently, the explicit bar contained in s. 479-A(6) came into effect, prohibiting the High Court from using the general procedure under s. 476.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that because the appellants' offense of filing false affidavits fell under the scope of s. 479-A, the High Court was required to follow the special procedure laid down in that section. Since it did not, the initiation of proceedings under the general provision of s. 476 was legally barred by s. 479-A(6). Therefore, the action taken by the High Court was invalid.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the offence committed by the appellants by making false declarations in their affidavits fell under ss. 191/192 of the Indian Penal Code (giving/fabricating false evidence) or under s. 199 of the Indian Penal Code (false statement in a declaration).
appellant_arguments: The act of swearing false affidavits, which were intended to be used as evidence in a judicial proceeding to mislead the court, constitutes the offence of fabricating false evidence under ss. 191/192 of the Indian Penal Code.
respondent_arguments: The offence committed by the appellants was making a false statement in a declaration, which is specifically covered by s. 199 of the Indian Penal Code. (This argument is inferred from the High Court's ruling in their favor, as the respondents were not represented in the Supreme Court).

arguments.issue_text: Whether proceedings for giving false evidence could be initiated under s. 476 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, or whether such action was barred because the specific procedure under s. 479-A of the Code was not followed.
appellant_arguments: Since the offence falls under ss. 191/192 IPC (fabricating false evidence) and was committed by a witness in a judicial proceeding, the special procedure laid down in s. 479-A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is the only one that can be followed.

As the High Court did not follow the mandatory procedure of s. 479-A at the time of disposing of the proceeding, initiating a prosecution later under the general provision of s. 476 of the Code is explicitly barred.
respondent_arguments: The general procedure under s. 476 of the Code of Criminal Procedure could be invoked because the special procedure under s. 479-A did not apply to an offence under s. 199 of the Indian Penal Code. (This argument is inferred from the High Court's acceptance of their application under s. 476).

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Making a false declaration in an affidavit intended to be used as evidence in a judicial proceeding constitutes an offense of giving or fabricating false evidence under sections 191/192 of the Indian Penal Code, not an offense under section 199. The procedure for prosecution for such an offense is governed exclusively by the special provisions of section 479-A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and the general procedure under section 476 is barred.
obiter: Section 199 of the Indian Penal Code deals with a declaration that is not required to be on oath, but must be capable of being used as evidence which a court is bound or authorized by law to receive.
Section 191 of the Indian Penal Code deals with evidence given on oath.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the appellants' act of making false declarations in affidavits, which were intended to be used as evidence to mislead the High Court, constituted the offence of fabricating false evidence under ss. 191/192 of the Indian Penal Code, rather than the lesser offence of making a false statement in a declaration under s. 199. Consequently, any prosecution for this offence, when committed by a witness in a judicial proceeding, must exclusively follow the special procedure laid down in s. 479-A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Since the High Court failed to follow this mandatory procedure at the time of its final order, it was subsequently barred from initiating a prosecution under the general provisions of s. 476 of the Code.
legal_tests_applied: The principle that a special procedural law (s. 479-A CrPC) overrides and excludes a general procedural law (s. 476 CrPC) for the specific offences it covers.

The test to distinguish between offences is intent: if a false declaration is made with the intention that it appear in evidence and cause a court to form an erroneous opinion, the offence falls under ss. 191/192 IPC (fabricating false evidence), not s. 199 IPC (false statement in a declaration).

The procedural requirement under s. 479-A CrPC is mandatory: for offences of giving or fabricating false evidence by a witness, the court must record a finding and initiate a complaint 'at the time of the delivery of the judgment or final order disposing of such proceeding'. Failure to do so bars a later prosecution under s. 476.
policy_considerations: The special procedure in s. 479-A of the Code of Criminal Procedure was specifically enacted 'for the eradication of the evils of perjury' by enabling courts to take swift and decisive action against witnesses who give or fabricate false evidence during a proceeding.
